svg.title: The five ITIL service lifecycle stages looping back through continual improvement, and how ITIL divides the work with TOGAF
svg.desc: Five boxes run left to right: service strategy with demand and portfolio, service design with SLAs and capacity, service transition with build, test and release, service operation with incident, problem and change, and continual service improvement with measure, improve and repeat. A return path loops from the last box back to the first. Two panels below divide the work: TOGAF answers what the architecture should be, in Day 0 vocabulary of baseline, target, gap and roadmap, while ITIL answers how it is run, in Day 1 and Day 2 vocabulary of SLA, incident, change and capacity. A red note states that a design ignoring the operation stage hands Day 2 an unmanageable system, which is where the money is spent for the next five years.
svg.text: ITIL covers the half of the lifecycle TOGAF stops short of
One framework decides the shape; the other decides whether the shape can be run
continual service improvement closes the loop: operations feeds the next design
Day 0 vocabulary: baseline, target, gap, roadmap
How is it run, day by day?
Day 1 / Day 2 vocabulary: SLA, incident, change, capacity
deliverable: service design package, runbooks, staffed rota
decides whether the shape survives contact with Monday
A design that never sees the operation stage hands Day 2 an unmanageable system — and Day 2 is where the money goes for the next five years.
Complexity added on Day 0 is paid for every year afterwards, by people who did not choose it.
Ask both questions in the same review: can this be built (TOGAF), and can this be operated by the team we actually have (ITIL).
